text.hook:
"Is shared_ptr thread-safe?"
Yes and no are both wrong answers.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. Three layers, three questions
2. Safe and unsafe, case by case
3. Why one shared handle races
4. atomic<shared_ptr> and copy-on-write
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: What is thread-safe, what is not, and the answers that fail.

slides.title: Three layers, three questions

cards.label: The handle
cards.text: One `shared_ptr` variable shared by threads, with a writer? Needs a mutex or `atomic<shared_ptr>`.

cards.label: The lifetime
cards.text: Protected for every thread holding its **own** copy. Not for raw pointers or references.

cards.label: The object
cards.text: `shared_ptr` does nothing here. Immutable, a mutex, or atomic members.

slides.takeaway: `shared_ptr` makes ownership thread-safe. Not the handle variable, not the object.

slides.title: Safe or data race?
slides.takeaway: Same rule as `int`: const access from many threads is fine. A writer needs exclusion.

slides.title: Why copying `g` races
steps: Meanwhile another thread reassigns `g` and drops the last owner: block freed
Copy step 2: increment a count in **freed memory**
Fix: make "read + increment" one step: a mutex or `atomic<shared_ptr>`

slides.title: What it gives, what it costs
rows: libstdc++ from GCC 12. GCC 11 rejects it
slides.takeaway: One plain `sp = x` next to `atomic_load` breaks it. That is why C++20 made it a type.

slides.title: Two writers: the lost update

cards.label: The bug
cards.text: A and B both load v1, both build v2 from it, both store. One update is gone.

cards.label: Fix 1
cards.text: A mutex that serializes writers only. Readers stay on `load()`.

cards.label: Fix 2
cards.text: A CAS loop: `compare_exchange_weak` publishes only if nobody else did.

slides.takeaway: Readers: one `load()` per operation. Two loads can return two versions.

slides.hero:
No mutex does not
mean no cost.
slides.lead: Every copy is an atomic RMW on one cache line. Measured (GCC 11 -O2, x86-64): 8 threads on one block, about 20x slower per copy than one thread.

items.truth: Its control block is. The handle variable and the object are not.

items.myth: "It is not thread-safe, so every copy needs a mutex."
items.truth: Copies of each other in different threads are fine. Only a shared handle with a writer needs one.

items.myth: "If the race happens, the reader just sees the old or the new pointer."
items.truth: It is UB. Real failures: use-after-free inside the refcount.
Usually a lock bit inside. `is_lock_free()` is `false`.
Ordering is not atomicity. Repeated concurrent writes still race.
A `weak_ptr` in another thread can `lock()` right after the check.

slides.hero:
Own copy per thread:
safe.

One shared handle
+ a writer: race.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
The reference count is atomic.
One thread copies a global shared_ptr, another replaces it.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Most engineers answer this one from the word "atomic". The program disagrees.

slides.title: The count is atomic. Race-free?

slides.verdict_sub: TSan: data race, copy vs assignment. Observed (GCC 11, -O0): segfaults and "pure virtual method called"
bullets: Both threads touch the **same** `shared_ptr` object, and one writes it.
A copy reads two pointers, **then** increments the count.
In between, the writer can drop the last owner: the reader increments a freed block.
The atomic count protects copies of each other, not one shared handle.

slides.title: Copy and replace the handle under a mutex
slides.takeaway: Readers use their copy with no lock held. TSan: clean.

text.hook:
Each thread gets its own shared_ptr copy.
So the counter must be correct?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: At -O2 it may even print the right number. That is the dangerous part.

slides.title: Two handles. Correct count?

slides.verdict_sub: Prints at most 200000. Observed at -O0: 113544, 146620. TSan: data race on `fills`
bullets: The handles are separate, so the `shared_ptr` part is fine: lifetime is protected.
Both threads modify the **same** `Stats` with no synchronization.
`shared_ptr` never protects the object it points to.
At -O2 each loop may become one `+= 100000` and hide the bug. TSan still reports it.
slides.wrong: "Always 200000, each thread has its own copy"

slides.title: Make the shared data itself safe
slides.takeaway: Separate handles protect lifetime, not the pointee's data.

text.hook:
Config hot-reload with atomic<shared_ptr>.
The reader never writes, every load is atomic, TSan is quiet.
So it is correct. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: A classic system-design follow-up. This reader passes every unit test.

slides.title: What can go wrong?

slides.verdict_sub: Two `load()` calls can return two different configs
bullets: `max_qty` from v1, `max_px` from v2: a combination nobody configured.
Not B: `load()` returns an **owning** copy. A `store()` cannot free it under you.
Not D: readers only read, and `const Config` stops them from writing.
Rule: one `load()` per operation, read every field through it.
slides.wrong: "Every load is atomic, so the check is consistent"

slides.title: One snapshot per operation
bullets: Old configs die when their last reader drops its copy.
`atomic<shared_ptr>` is C++20: GCC 12+ (not GCC 11), and `is_lock_free()` is `false`.
slides.takeaway: Atomic handle + immutable object + one snapshot per operation.

text.hook:
main creates a big object. A reader thread holds a copy.
Which thread pays for destroying it?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: In low-latency code this decides who pays for freeing a big object.

slides.title: What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: Every run: `main` drops its copy first, the reader drops the last one
bullets: The decrement that reaches 0 runs the destructor right there, inline, on that thread.
Not the creator, not a library thread: reference counting has no thread of its own.
Shared snapshots: often a **reader on the hot path** frees a big old object.
Dropped inside a critical section: the destructor runs under the lock.
slides.wrong: "The thread that created it destroys it"

slides.title: Decide where the last release happens
bullets: Or a retire list freed on a background thread, or a deferred-free deleter.
slides.takeaway: The same holds for the control block: the last `weak_ptr` or owner frees it, on its own thread.
